heart.title: The Human Heart
heart.description: The heart is a muscular organ roughly the size of a closed fist, weighing between 250–350 grams. Located in the mediastinum of the thoracic cavity, it beats approximately 100,000 times per day, pumping around 7,570 litres of blood through 96,000 kilometres of blood vessels.

mesh_0.name: Heart — Full Structure
mesh_0.description: The human heart is a four-chambered muscular organ that serves as the primary pump of the cardiovascular system. Enclosed within the pericardial sac, it is positioned obliquely in the chest — approximately two-thirds to the left of the midline. The outer surface is covered by the epicardium and contains the coronary arteries and veins that supply the myocardium itself.
mesh_0.function: Generates the pressure gradient that drives systemic and pulmonary circulation. The right side receives deoxygenated blood from the body and pumps it to the lungs; the left side receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and pumps it to the entire body.
mesh_0.clinical: Heart failure, coronary artery disease, and arrhythmias are among the most common pathologies. Myocardial infarction (heart attack) occurs when coronary blood flow is obstructed.
facts: Beats ~100,000 times per day
Pumps ~7,570 litres of blood daily
The left ventricle wall is 3× thicker than the right
Your heart has its own electrical system (SA node, AV node)

left_ventricle.name: Left Ventricle
left_ventricle.description: The left ventricle is the thickest chamber of the heart, with walls approximately 1.3–1.5 cm thick. It forms the apex and the majority of the left border and diaphragmatic surface of the heart. Internally, it features trabeculae carneae (muscular ridges) and papillary muscles that anchor the chordae tendineae of the mitral valve.
left_ventricle.function: Receives oxygenated blood from the left atrium via the mitral valve and pumps it into the aorta at systemic arterial pressure (~120 mmHg during systole). This is the most powerful chamber.
left_ventricle.clinical: Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) is a common finding in chronic hypertension. Reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF < 40%) indicates heart failure with reduced function.
facts: Generates pressures up to 120 mmHg
Wall is ~3× thicker than right ventricle
Contains papillary muscles and trabeculae carneae
LVEF (ejection fraction) is a key cardiac health metric

right_ventricle.name: Right Ventricle
right_ventricle.description: The right ventricle is a crescent-shaped chamber that lies anterior to the left ventricle. Its walls are approximately 3–5 mm thick. It has a distinct inflow tract (from the tricuspid valve) and outflow tract (to the pulmonary valve), separated by the supraventricular crest.
right_ventricle.function: Receives deoxygenated blood from the right atrium and pumps it through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary artery for gas exchange in the lungs. It operates at much lower pressures (~25 mmHg) than the left ventricle.
right_ventricle.clinical: Right ventricular failure can result from pulmonary hypertension, tricuspid valve disease, or right ventricular infarction. Cor pulmonale refers to right heart failure due to lung disease.
facts: Operates at ~25 mmHg (much lower than left side)
Crescent-shaped in cross section
Contains moderator band (septomarginal trabeculation)
Anterior-most chamber of the heart

left_atrium.name: Left Atrium
left_atrium.description: The left atrium is a thin-walled, smooth-surfaced chamber located posteriorly. It receives four pulmonary veins (two from each lung) carrying oxygenated blood. The left atrial appendage (auricle) is a remnant of the embryonic atrium and a common site for thrombus formation in atrial fibrillation.
left_atrium.function: Collects oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins and delivers it to the left ventricle through the mitral (bicuspid) valve during ventricular diastole.
left_atrium.clinical: Left atrial enlargement is common in mitral valve disease and atrial fibrillation. The left atrial appendage is the most frequent site of thrombus formation in AF patients.
facts: Receives blood from four pulmonary veins
Most posterior chamber of the heart
Left atrial appendage is a common clot site
Pressure: ~8-12 mmHg normally

right_atrium.name: Right Atrium
right_atrium.description: The right atrium forms the right border of the heart and receives systemic venous return. The superior vena cava enters superiorly, the inferior vena cava enters inferiorly, and the coronary sinus drains the cardiac veins posteroinferiorly. Internally, the crista terminalis separates the smooth sinus venarum from the ridged pectinate muscles of the auricle.
right_atrium.function: Receives deoxygenated blood from the systemic circulation (via the SVC, IVC, and coronary sinus) and passes it to the right ventricle through the tricuspid valve.
right_atrium.clinical: Atrial septal defect (ASD) creates an abnormal communication between the right and left atria. Right atrial enlargement can occur in tricuspid valve disease or pulmonary hypertension.
facts: Contains the SA node (pacemaker of the heart)
Has smooth and rough (pectinate) regions
Receives blood from SVC, IVC, and coronary sinus
Interatrial septum contains the fossa ovalis

aorta.name: Aorta
aorta.description: The aorta is the largest artery in the human body, approximately 2.5 cm in diameter at its origin. It arises from the left ventricle, ascends, arches posteriorly over the left main bronchus (the aortic arch), then descends through the thorax and abdomen. The aortic root contains the sinuses of Valsalva, from which the coronary arteries originate.
aorta.function: Primary high-pressure conduit that distributes oxygenated blood to every region of the body. The elastic walls stretch during systole and recoil during diastole, smoothing pulsatile flow (the Windkessel effect).
aorta.clinical: Aortic aneurysm (abnormal dilation) can be life-threatening if ruptured. Aortic dissection occurs when blood enters the medial layer. Aortic stenosis and regurgitation affect the aortic valve.
facts: Largest artery — ~2.5 cm diameter
Aortic arch gives off brachiocephalic, left common carotid, and left subclavian arteries
Coronary arteries originate from the aortic root
Elastic walls create the Windkessel effect

pulmonary_artery.name: Pulmonary Artery
pulmonary_artery.description: The pulmonary trunk emerges from the right ventricle and bifurcates into the left and right pulmonary arteries, which carry deoxygenated blood to the respective lungs. Unlike systemic arteries, pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood. The pulmonary trunk is approximately 5 cm long before splitting.
pulmonary_artery.function: Transports deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs for gas exchange. It forms the beginning of the pulmonary circulation where CO₂ is released and O₂ is absorbed.
pulmonary_artery.clinical: Pulmonary embolism (PE) occurs when a clot lodges in the pulmonary arteries, blocking blood flow. Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a progressive condition with elevated pressures in the pulmonary vasculature.
facts: Only arteries that carry deoxygenated blood
Pulmonary trunk is ~5 cm long
Pressure: ~25/8 mmHg (much lower than systemic)
Bifurcates into left and right pulmonary arteries

superior_vena_cava.name: Superior Vena Cava
superior_vena_cava.description: The superior vena cava (SVC) is formed by the union of the left and right brachiocephalic veins. It descends vertically to enter the right atrium at the level of the third costal cartilage. It drains the head, neck, upper limbs, and thorax. It has no valves.
superior_vena_cava.function: Returns deoxygenated blood from the upper half of the body (head, neck, arms, and upper thorax) to the right atrium.
superior_vena_cava.clinical: SVC syndrome results from obstruction or compression of the SVC, often by malignancy (e.g., lung cancer, lymphoma). Symptoms include facial swelling, dyspnea, and distended neck veins.
facts: ~7 cm long
Has no valves
Formed by union of brachiocephalic veins
SVC syndrome is a medical emergency

inferior_vena_cava.name: Inferior Vena Cava
inferior_vena_cava.description: The inferior vena cava (IVC) is the largest vein in the body, formed by the confluence of the left and right common iliac veins at the level of L5. It ascends through the abdomen, pierces the diaphragm at the caval opening (T8), and enters the right atrium from below.
inferior_vena_cava.function: Returns deoxygenated blood from the lower half of the body (legs, pelvis, abdomen) and abdominal organs to the right atrium. It receives hepatic, renal, adrenal, and iliac venous tributaries.
inferior_vena_cava.clinical: IVC thrombosis can cause lower limb edema and renal complications. IVC filters are sometimes placed to prevent pulmonary embolism in patients with deep vein thrombosis.
facts: Largest vein in the human body
Pierces diaphragm at T8 vertebral level
Receives venous drainage from most abdominal organs
IVC filters can prevent pulmonary embolism

mitral_valve.name: Mitral Valve (Bicuspid Valve)
mitral_valve.description: The mitral valve is a bicuspid (two-leaflet) valve located between the left atrium and left ventricle. It has anterior and posterior leaflets attached by chordae tendineae to the anterolateral and posteromedial papillary muscles. It prevents backflow of blood into the left atrium during ventricular systole.
mitral_valve.function: Opens during diastole to allow blood to flow from the left atrium into the left ventricle. Closes during systole to prevent regurgitation. Normal mitral valve area is 4–6 cm².
mitral_valve.clinical: Mitral stenosis (often rheumatic) restricts flow. Mitral regurgitation allows backflow. Mitral valve prolapse is the most common valvular abnormality, where leaflets billow into the atrium.
facts: Only valve with 2 leaflets (bicuspid)
Normal area: 4–6 cm²
Chordae tendineae prevent leaflet eversion
Mitral valve prolapse affects ~2-3% of population

tricuspid_valve.name: Tricuspid Valve
tricuspid_valve.description: The tricuspid valve has three leaflets (anterior, posterior, and septal) and is located between the right atrium and right ventricle. It is larger than the mitral valve and has chordae tendineae connected to three papillary muscles.
tricuspid_valve.function: Permits unidirectional blood flow from the right atrium to the right ventricle during diastole and prevents backflow during systole.
tricuspid_valve.clinical: Tricuspid regurgitation is common in pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure. Tricuspid valve endocarditis is associated with IV drug use.
facts: Three leaflets: anterior, posterior, septal
Largest cardiac valve by diameter
Endocarditis here often linked to IV drug use
Functional regurgitation common in heart failure

coronary_arteries.name: Coronary Arteries
coronary_arteries.description: The coronary arteries are the first branches of the aorta, originating from the sinuses of Valsalva just above the aortic valve. The left coronary artery (LCA) bifurcates into the left anterior descending (LAD) and left circumflex (LCx) arteries. The right coronary artery (RCA) supplies the right ventricle and typically the inferior wall of the left ventricle.
coronary_arteries.function: Supply the myocardium with oxygenated blood. The heart muscle requires continuous perfusion — cardiac extraction of oxygen from coronary blood is ~75%, the highest of any organ.
coronary_arteries.clinical: Coronary artery disease (CAD) is the leading cause of death worldwide. Atherosclerotic plaque buildup narrows the lumen, reducing myocardial perfusion. Complete occlusion causes myocardial infarction (heart attack).
facts: Heart extracts ~75% of oxygen from coronary blood
LAD supplies ~50% of left ventricular mass
Coronary blood flow occurs mainly during diastole
CAD is the #1 cause of death globally

quiz.question: How many chambers does the human heart have?
quiz.explanation: The human heart has four chambers: two atria (upper chambers) and two ventricles (lower chambers).

quiz.question: Which chamber of the heart has the thickest walls?
quiz.explanation: The left ventricle has the thickest walls (~1.3–1.5 cm) because it must generate enough pressure to pump blood through the entire systemic circulation.

quiz.question: What is the function of the mitral valve?
options: Prevents backflow from the aorta into the left ventricle
Prevents backflow from the left ventricle into the left atrium
Prevents backflow from the right ventricle into the right atrium
Prevents backflow from the pulmonary artery into the right ventricle
quiz.explanation: The mitral (bicuspid) valve sits between the left atrium and left ventricle, preventing blood from flowing back into the left atrium during ventricular contraction.

quiz.question: Which vessel carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs?
quiz.explanation: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs for gas exchange. It is the only artery that carries deoxygenated blood.

quiz.question: Where do the coronary arteries originate?
quiz.explanation: The coronary arteries originate from the sinuses of Valsalva in the aortic root, just above the aortic valve.

quiz.question: Approximately how many times does the heart beat per day?
quiz.explanation: The heart beats approximately 100,000 times per day, pumping around 7,570 litres of blood.

quiz.question: What is the natural pacemaker of the heart?
quiz.explanation: The sinoatrial (SA) node, located in the right atrium, is the natural pacemaker. It generates electrical impulses that initiate each heartbeat.

quiz.question: The LAD artery supplies approximately what percentage of the left ventricular mass?
quiz.explanation: The left anterior descending (LAD) artery supplies approximately 50% of the left ventricular myocardial mass, making it critically important.

quiz.question: What is the Windkessel effect?
options: The electrical conduction through the heart
The elastic recoil of the aorta smoothing pulsatile blood flow
The contraction of the papillary muscles
The opening of the semilunar valves
quiz.explanation: The Windkessel effect refers to the elastic properties of the aorta and large arteries that stretch during systole and recoil during diastole, converting pulsatile flow into smoother continuous flow.

quiz.question: Which valve has only two leaflets?
quiz.explanation: The mitral valve (also called the bicuspid valve) is the only cardiac valve with two leaflets. All other valves have three.

lungs.title: The Lungs & Respiratory System
lungs.description: The lungs are a pair of spongy, air-filled organs located on either side of the chest (thorax). The trachea (windpipe) conducts inhaled air into the lungs through its tubular branches, called bronchi, which then branch into smaller bronchioles leading to microscopic air sacs called alveoli where gas exchange occurs.

left_lung.name: Left Lung
left_lung.description: The left lung is slightly smaller than the right lung to accommodate the heart (cardiac notch). It is divided into two lobes: the superior lobe and inferior lobe, separated by the oblique fissure.
left_lung.function: Facilitates gas exchange. Oxygen enters the bloodstream from inhaled air, and carbon dioxide is removed from blood to be exhaled. Due to the cardiac notch, the left lung has about 10% less capacity than the right.
left_lung.clinical: Pneumonia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and asthma commonly affect lung tissues, reducing surface area or causing airway constriction. Left-sided lung infections can spread to the pleural cavity (pleurisy).
facts: Smaller than the right lung due to the heart's position
Has 2 lobes (superior and inferior)
Contains the cardiac notch on its anterior border
Separated by a single oblique fissure

right_lung.name: Right Lung
right_lung.description: The right lung is shorter but wider than the left lung, and has a larger overall capacity. It is divided into three lobes: superior, middle, and inferior lobes, separated by the horizontal and oblique fissures.
right_lung.function: Enables respiration and gas exchange. Its larger volume allows it to perform approximately 55% of total pulmonary gas exchange under normal conditions.
right_lung.clinical: Right lung aspiration is clinically common because the right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical than the left main bronchus. Foreign objects are more likely to lodge here.
facts: Has 3 lobes (superior, middle, inferior)
Larger and heavier than the left lung
Separated by horizontal and oblique fissures
Positioned slightly higher to accommodate the liver underneath

trachea.name: Trachea (Windpipe)
trachea.description: The trachea is a cartilaginous tube that connects the larynx to the bronchi. It is reinforced by 16-20 C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage, which prevent it from collapsing during inhalation.
trachea.function: Serves as the main airway passage. Lined with ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium, it sweeps mucus and trapped foreign particles upward away from the lungs (mucociliary escalator).
trachea.clinical: Tracheostomy is a surgical procedure to create an airway opening in the trachea during severe upper airway obstruction. Intubation guides a tube through the trachea to support mechanical ventilation.
facts: Reinforced by 16-20 C-shaped cartilaginous rings
Lined with ciliated cells to filter air
Approximately 10-11 cm long in adults
Prevents collapsing under negative pressure during breathing

bronchi.name: Bronchial Tree
bronchi.description: At the carina, the trachea divides into the right and left primary (main) bronchi. These enter the lungs at the hilum and branch into secondary (lobar) bronchi, tertiary (segmental) bronchi, and eventually bronchioles.
bronchi.function: Conducts air into the individual lobes and segments of the lungs. The walls contain smooth muscle that can constrict (bronchoconstriction) or dilate (bronchodilation) to regulate airflow resistance.
bronchi.clinical: Asthma is characterized by chronic inflammation and hyperreactivity of the bronchioles, leading to bronchospasm. Bronchitis is an inflammation of the bronchial lining, causing mucus buildup.
facts: Right main bronchus is wider and more vertical than the left
Branching forms a tree-like network of airways
Bronchi contain cartilage, while bronchioles lack cartilage
Controlled by autonomic nervous system to dilate/constrict

alveoli.name: Alveoli (Air Sacs)
alveoli.description: Alveoli are microscopic, grape-like air sacs at the terminal ends of the bronchioles. They are surrounded by an extensive network of pulmonary capillaries. The alveolar wall consists of Type I (gas exchange) and Type II (surfactant-producing) pneumocytes.
alveoli.function: The primary site of gas exchange in the respiratory system. Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across the thin respiratory membrane (less than 0.5 micrometres thick) down their partial pressure gradients.
alveoli.clinical: Emphysema (part of COPD) destroys alveolar walls, reducing the surface area for gas exchange. Pulmonary surfactant deficiency in premature infants causes Infant Respiratory Distress Syndrome (IRDS).
facts: Human lungs contain ~300-500 million alveoli
Total surface area is roughly equivalent to a tennis court (~70-100 m²)
Type II alveolar cells secrete surfactant to reduce surface tension
Alveolar membrane is extremely thin (<0.5 microns) for rapid diffusion

quiz.question: How many lobes does the left lung have?
quiz.explanation: The left lung has two lobes (superior and inferior) to make room for the heart, whereas the right lung has three lobes.

quiz.question: Why are inhaled foreign objects more likely to enter the right lung than the left?
options: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical
The left lung cardiac notch blocks foreign particles
Gravity pulls objects to the right
quiz.explanation: The right primary bronchus is wider, shorter, and runs more vertically than the left, making it the most common destination for aspirated foreign bodies.

quiz.question: What is the primary site of gas exchange in the lungs?
quiz.explanation: Alveoli are the microscopic air sacs where oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse between the lungs and the surrounding blood capillaries.

quiz.question: Which cells produce pulmonary surfactant to prevent alveolar collapse?
quiz.explanation: Type II alveolar cells (pneumocytes) secrete surfactant, a lipid-protein mixture that reduces surface tension in the alveoli, preventing them from collapsing during exhalation.

quiz.question: What cartilaginous structure reinforces the trachea to keep it open?
quiz.explanation: The trachea is held open by C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage. The open part of the 'C' faces posteriorly, allowing the esophagus to expand slightly when food is swallowed.

liver.title: The Liver & Gallbladder
liver.description: The liver is the largest internal organ in the body, weighing about 1.5 kilograms. Positioned in the upper right quadrant of the abdomen, it performs over 500 vital functions, including chemical detoxification, protein synthesis, glycogen storage, and the production of bile for fat digestion.

right_lobe.name: Right Lobe of the Liver
right_lobe.description: The right lobe is the largest lobe of the liver, accounting for about five-sixths of the organ's total mass. It is separated from the left lobe on the anterior surface by the falciform ligament.
right_lobe.function: Houses the bulk of the hepatocytes (liver cells) responsible for metabolizing carbohydrates, lipids, and proteins, filtering toxic substances, and synthesizing bile.
right_lobe.clinical: Liver cirrhosis, often caused by chronic alcohol abuse or hepatitis infections, leads to progressive scarring and loss of function. The right lobe is the primary target for biopsy and resection.
facts: Accounts for ~5/6 of the liver's total mass
Separated from left lobe by the falciform ligament
Contains caudate and quadrate lobes on its visceral surface
Has an extremely high capacity for cellular regeneration

left_lobe.name: Left Lobe of the Liver
left_lobe.description: The left lobe is much smaller than the right lobe, flattened from side to side, and situated mainly in the epigastric region of the abdomen. It has a smooth upper surface that fits under the diaphragm.
left_lobe.function: Performs identical metabolic, storage, and secretory functions as the right lobe, but on a smaller scale due to its size.
left_lobe.clinical: Due to the liver's dual blood supply and segmental anatomy, the left lobe can be harvested from a living donor for transplant into a child or small adult, and both the donor's and recipient's segments will regenerate to full size.
facts: Situated in the epigastric and left hypochondriac regions
Much smaller and thinner than the right lobe
Can be safely donated for living-donor transplants
Regenerates to normal volume within weeks after partial resection

gallbladder.name: Gallbladder
gallbladder.description: The gallbladder is a small, pear-shaped muscular sac located in a shallow depression on the inferior surface of the liver's right lobe. It connects to the biliary system via the cystic duct.
gallbladder.function: Stores and concentrates bile produced by the liver. When fatty food enters the duodenum, the hormone cholecystokinin (CCK) triggers gallbladder contraction, expelling bile into the common bile duct to emulsify fats.
gallbladder.clinical: Cholelithiasis (gallstones) can form when bile contains too much cholesterol or bilirubin. Obstruction of the cystic duct leads to cholecystitis (acute inflammation), which often requires surgical removal (cholecystectomy).
facts: Stores and concentrates bile (does not produce it)
Contraction is triggered by the hormone cholecystokinin (CCK)
Pear-shaped sac ~7-10 cm long
Can be removed without major impact on digestion (liver still drains bile)

hepatic_portal.name: Hepatic Portal Vein
hepatic_portal.description: The hepatic portal vein is a large blood vessel formed by the confluence of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins. It carries blood from the gastrointestinal tract, spleen, and pancreas to the liver.
hepatic_portal.function: Supplies the liver with ~75% of its total blood volume. This blood is rich in nutrients and toxins absorbed from the digestive tract, which the liver processes and purifies before it returns to systemic circulation.
hepatic_portal.clinical: Portal hypertension (elevated pressure in the portal system) is a severe complication of liver cirrhosis, leading to ascites (fluid in the abdomen) and life-threatening esophageal varices (bleeding veins).
facts: Supplies ~75% of the liver's blood flow (but carries deoxygenated blood)
Formed by splenic and superior mesenteric veins
Delivers absorbed nutrients directly to hepatocytes
Obstruction leads to portal hypertension

quiz.question: What is the primary function of the gallbladder?
quiz.explanation: The gallbladder does not produce bile (the liver does). It stores and concentrates bile, releasing it into the small intestine to help digest fats.

quiz.question: Which vessel supplies the majority of blood flow to the liver?
quiz.explanation: The hepatic portal vein supplies about 75% of the liver's blood flow, delivering nutrient-rich but oxygen-poor blood directly from the digestive tract.

quiz.question: What hormone triggers the gallbladder to contract and release bile?
quiz.explanation: Cholecystokinin (CCK) is released by cells in the duodenum in response to fatty foods, triggering gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion.

quiz.question: What is the medical term for gallstone formation?
quiz.explanation: Cholelithiasis is the presence of gallstones, which are crystallized deposits of bile components (such as cholesterol or calcium salts) in the gallbladder.

quiz.question: What ligament separates the left and right lobes of the liver on its anterior surface?
quiz.explanation: The falciform ligament is a broad, thin fold of peritoneum that attaches the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm, separating the right and left lobes.

all.title: Combined Thoracic & Abdominal Anatomy
all.description: An interactive 3D map showing the spatial, structural, and circulatory relationships between the Heart, Lungs, and Liver within the upper body cavity.

heart.name: The Heart
heart.description: Positioned obliquely in the mediastinum between the two lungs. Serves as the central pump of the cardiovascular system.
heart.function: Pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs for oxygenation and pumps oxygen-rich blood to the rest of the body, including the liver.
heart.clinical: Heart failure causes fluid backflow; left-sided failure causes pulmonary congestion (lungs), while right-sided failure leads to systemic congestion (enlarged liver/hepatomegaly).
facts: Positioned in the middle mediastinum
Flanked on either side by the lungs
Rests on the central tendon of the diaphragm
Interacts dynamically with lungs and liver via circulation

left_lung.name: The Lungs (Respiration)
left_lung.description: Spongy respiratory organs that flank the heart. The right lung sits slightly higher due to the massive liver located immediately below the diaphragm.
left_lung.function: Responsible for oxygenating blood received from the heart and removing carbon dioxide before sending blood back to the left atrium.
left_lung.clinical: Pulmonary embolism blocks blood flow from the heart to the lungs. Emphysema reduces the area available for gas exchange, forcing the heart to pump harder.
facts: Receive deoxygenated blood from the pulmonary trunk
Return oxygenated blood to the left atrium
Envelop the heart in the thoracic cavity
Supported from below by the diaphragm muscle

liver.name: The Liver (Metabolism)
liver.description: The largest internal organ, situated in the upper right quadrant of the abdomen directly beneath the diaphragm and inferior to the heart and lungs.
liver.function: Processes blood from the digestive tract via the hepatic portal system and receives oxygenated blood from the heart via the hepatic artery.
liver.clinical: Congestive heart failure leads to passive congestion of the liver, causing abdominal pain and abnormal liver function tests (cardiac cirrhosis).
facts: Largest abdominal organ
Located directly below the diaphragm and right lung
Drains into the inferior vena cava (IVC) via hepatic veins
Processes all nutrients and toxins entering through digestion

brain.name: The Brain (Central Control)
brain.description: Located within the cranium, the brain serves as the primary processing hub of the nervous system, coordinating consciousness, motor commands, and homeostatic reflex loops.
brain.function: Governs systemic neural control, autonomic tone, sensory perception, and cognitive thought.
brain.clinical: Stroke, traumatic brain injury, and neurodegenerative diseases disrupt central regulation.
facts: Consumes 20% of resting cardiac output and oxygen
Contains 86 billion interconnected neurons
Communicates with peripheral organs via the spinal cord and autonomic nerves
Protected by the blood-brain barrier and cerebrospinal fluid

kidneys.name: The Kidneys (Excretion & Fluid Balance)
kidneys.description: Paired retroperitoneal organs flanking the vertebral column in the posterior abdomen, functioning as the primary filtration and volume-regulatory organs.
kidneys.function: Filters nitrogenous wastes, balances blood pH and electrolyte osmolarity, and modulates systemic blood pressure.
kidneys.clinical: Chronic kidney disease impairs fluid clearance, leading to hypertension and secondary cardiovascular strain.
facts: Filters 180 liters of blood plasma daily
Produces erythropoietin (EPO) to stimulate red blood cell synthesis
Secretes renin to regulate arterial blood pressure
Operates in tandem with heart and liver in fluid-electrolyte balance

quiz.question: Which organ consumes approximately 20% of the body's total oxygen and glucose despite accounting for only 2% of body mass?
quiz.explanation: The brain represents roughly 2% of total body weight (~1.4 kg) yet consumes around 20% of resting oxygen and glucose metabolism due to constant neuronal ion pump activity.

quiz.question: Which paired organs filter ~180 liters of blood plasma per day to regulate fluid balance and blood pressure?
quiz.explanation: The kidneys filter approximately 180 liters of filtrate each day through glomerular capillary beds, reabsorbing over 99% of fluid back into systemic circulation.

quiz.question: Which clinical condition connects right heart failure directly with liver pathology?
quiz.explanation: Right ventricular failure elevates systemic venous pressure in the IVC and hepatic veins, causing retrograde blood congestion in hepatic sinusoids known as nutmeg liver or congestive hepatomegaly.

quiz.question: Where does oxygen-rich blood returning from the lungs enter the heart?
quiz.explanation: Oxygenated blood flows from the pulmonary capillary beds through the pulmonary veins directly into the left atrium of the heart.

quiz.question: What vascular conduit delivers 75% of blood flow carrying absorbed nutrients from the gut to the liver?
quiz.explanation: The hepatic portal vein collects venous drainage from the stomach, intestines, pancreas, and spleen, delivering nutrient-rich blood straight to hepatocytes for metabolic processing.

brain.title: The Human Brain
brain.description: The human brain is the central command center of the nervous system, comprising ~86 billion neurons and over 100 trillion synapses. Consuming 20% of the body's total metabolic energy despite weighing only 1.4 kg, it governs conscious thought, emotion, memory, motor coordination, and vital autonomic homeostasis.

cerebrum.name: Cerebrum (Cerebral Cortex)
cerebrum.description: The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain, divided into left and right hemispheres connected by the corpus callosum. The outer gray matter cortex is heavily folded into gyri (ridges) and sulci (grooves) to dramatically expand its surface area.
cerebrum.function: Governs higher cognitive functions, conscious perception, abstract reasoning, language processing, complex memory integration, and voluntary motor planning.
cerebrum.clinical: Cerebrovascular accident (ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke) in cerebral arteries can cause localized hemiparesis, aphasia, or cognitive deficits depending on the vascular territory affected.
facts: Makes up ~85% of total brain mass
Divided into four primary lobes per hemisphere
Contains approximately 16 billion cortical neurons
Folded surface area equals ~2.5 square meters if unfolded

frontal_lobe.name: Frontal Lobe
frontal_lobe.description: Positioned directly behind the forehead, the frontal lobe is the largest lobe of the cerebral cortex. It houses the prefrontal cortex, the primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus), and Broca's speech area in the dominant hemisphere.
frontal_lobe.function: Controls executive functioning (decision making, impulse control, working memory), personality expression, voluntary movement initiation, and motor articulation of speech.
frontal_lobe.clinical: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) presents with pronounced personality changes and behavioral disinhibition. Damage to Broca's area leads to expressive (non-fluent) aphasia.
facts: Last region of the human brain to fully mature (~age 25)
Houses Broca's area for expressive speech production
Prefrontal cortex is the seat of executive decision making
Primary motor strip maps the body via the motor homunculus

parietal_lobe.name: Parietal Lobe
parietal_lobe.description: Located superiorly between the frontal and occipital lobes, posterior to the central sulcus. Contains the primary somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus) and association areas.
parietal_lobe.function: Processes sensory modalities including touch, temperature, nociception (pain), proprioception, and constructs three-dimensional spatial orientation and somatic body schema.
parietal_lobe.clinical: Lesions in the non-dominant (usually right) parietal lobe frequently cause contralateral hemispatial neglect, where patients fail to perceive stimuli on the left side of space.
facts: Contains the somatosensory homunculus for tactile mapping
Integrates multisensory data to form spatial awareness
Gerstmann syndrome results from dominant angular gyrus lesions
Crucial for mathematical calculations and body schema

temporal_lobe.name: Temporal Lobe
temporal_lobe.description: Situated inferior to the lateral fissure on both hemispheres, adjacent to the temples. Houses the primary auditory cortex, Wernicke's speech comprehension area, and the medial hippocampus.
temporal_lobe.function: Processes auditory signals, decodes receptive speech, interprets complex visual memories (faces, objects), and facilitates long-term declarative memory encoding via the hippocampus.
temporal_lobe.clinical: Damage to Wernicke's area in the dominant temporal lobe results in receptive (fluent) aphasia. Medial temporal lobe sclerosis is the most common cause of intractable temporal lobe epilepsy.
facts: Houses the hippocampus, essential for memory consolidation
Contains Wernicke's area for receptive language comprehension
Processes auditory frequency mapping (tonotopy)
Fusiform face area enables facial recognition

occipital_lobe.name: Occipital Lobe
occipital_lobe.description: The smallest of the four lobes, situated at the posterior pole of the cerebrum beneath the parieto-occipital sulcus. Contains the primary visual cortex (Brodmann area 17/V1) surrounding the calcarine sulcus.
occipital_lobe.function: Processes all visual input received from the retina via the optic radiations, resolving edges, orientation, color, depth perception, spatial frequency, and visual motion.
occipital_lobe.clinical: Posterior cerebral artery (PCA) stroke leads to contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing due to collateral blood supply from the middle cerebral artery.
facts: Primary destination for retina signals via the optic tract
Calcarine sulcus organizes retinotopic visual field maps
Visual processing splits into 'where' dorsal and 'what' ventral streams
Damage can produce cortical blindness without retinal pathology

cerebellum.name: Cerebellum ('Little Brain')
cerebellum.description: A compact structure tucked beneath the occipital lobes at the posterior cranial fossa. Despite making up only 10% of brain volume, it contains over 50% of all neurons in the entire central nervous system.
cerebellum.function: Coordinates voluntary motor movements, refines motor timing, maintains equilibrium and posture, and mediates motor error correction and muscle memory learning.
cerebellum.clinical: Cerebellar ataxia manifests as intention tremor, dysmetria (past-pointing), dysdiadochokinesia (impaired rapid alternating movements), and wide-based drunken gait.
facts: Contains more than half of the total neurons in the brain
Purkinje cells have the most elaborate dendritic arbors in biology
Does not initiate movement, but modulates and refines precision
Connected to brainstem by superior, middle, and inferior peduncles

brainstem.name: Brainstem (Midbrain, Pons & Medulla)
brainstem.description: The stalk-like structure connecting the cerebral hemispheres to the spinal cord. Composed of three contiguous segments: midbrain (mesencephalon), pons, and medulla oblongata.
brainstem.function: Regulates essential autonomic life-support reflexes (respiratory drive, cardiac rhythm, arterial blood pressure, swallowing, vomiting) and houses cranial nerve nuclei III through XII.
brainstem.clinical: Brainstem strokes or herniation (e.g. uncal or tonsillar herniation) can rapidly cause coma, decerebrate posturing, respiratory arrest, and brain death.
facts: Continuous with the spinal cord at the foramen magnum
Contains the reticular activating system (RAS) controlling consciousness
Houses the cardiorespiratory control centers in the medulla
Origin of 10 of the 12 pairs of cranial nerves

quiz.question: Which brain structure contains over 50% of the brain's total neurons despite accounting for only 10% of its volume?
quiz.explanation: The cerebellum contains an extraordinary density of granule and Purkinje neurons, packing more than half of all neurons in the brain into just 10% of its volume.

quiz.question: What speech disorder is characterized by impaired fluency but intact comprehension, typically caused by lesions in the left inferior frontal gyrus?
quiz.explanation: Broca's aphasia (expressive aphasia) occurs when Broca's area in the frontal lobe is injured. Patients understand language well but struggle to articulate grammatically coherent speech.

quiz.question: Which vital brainstem region houses the autonomic centers that regulate heart rate, blood pressure, and respiratory rhythm?
quiz.explanation: The medulla oblongata at the base of the brainstem contains the medullary respiratory center and cardiovascular control centers regulating resting heart rate and arterial pressure.

quiz.question: Where is the primary visual cortex (Brodmann area 17) anatomically located?
options: Occipital Lobe along the Calcarine Sulcus
quiz.explanation: The primary visual cortex resides in the occipital lobe bordering the calcarine fissure, receiving retinotopic visual inputs from the lateral geniculate nucleus.

quiz.question: Which lobe is primarily responsible for processing tactile sensations, proprioception, and constructing spatial orientation?
quiz.explanation: The parietal lobe contains the primary somatosensory cortex and multisensory association regions that integrate touch, temperature, position sense, and 3D space.

kidneys.title: The Kidneys & Renal System
kidneys.description: The human kidneys are bean-shaped retroperitoneal organs located along the posterior abdominal wall on either side of the vertebral column (T12–L3). Receiving roughly 20-25% of total cardiac output, they filter 180 liters of blood per day to excrete metabolic wastes, stabilize extracellular fluid volume, regulate blood pressure via the RAAS axis, and stimulate erythropoiesis.

renal_cortex.name: Renal Cortex
renal_cortex.description: The pale, granular outer layer of the kidney extending from the renal capsule inward between the medullary pyramids as the renal columns of Bertin.
renal_cortex.function: Houses approximately 1 million nephrons, containing all renal corpuscles (Bowman's capsules and glomeruli), proximal convoluted tubules, and distal convoluted tubules for ultrafiltration.
renal_cortex.clinical: Glomerulonephritis is an inflammatory disease affecting glomerular filtration barriers in the cortex, manifesting with hematuria, proteinuria, and acute renal failure.
facts: Receives ~85-90% of total renal blood flow
Contains all the glomeruli and Bowman's capsules
Extends columns between pyramids (columns of Bertin)
Primary site of ultrafiltration and tubular reabsorption

renal_medulla.name: Renal Medulla & Pyramids
renal_medulla.description: The inner, darker striated zone of the kidney divided into 8 to 18 conical renal pyramids. The bases face the cortex while the apices (renal papillae) point toward the renal sinus.
renal_medulla.function: Houses the long loops of Henle and medullary collecting ducts. Generates a steep hyperosmotic corticomedullary concentration gradient essential for water reabsorption under vasopressin (ADH).
renal_medulla.clinical: Renal papillary necrosis can occur in sickle cell disease, severe diabetes mellitus, or chronic analgesic abuse, leading to sloughed papillae causing ureteral obstruction.
facts: Composed of 8 to 18 striated renal pyramids
Features hypertonic interstitium reaching up to 1200 mOsm/L
Crucial for urine concentration via the countercurrent multiplier
Papillae drain directly into minor calyces

renal_pelvis.name: Renal Pelvis & Calyces
renal_pelvis.description: A wide, funnel-shaped sac in the renal sinus that receives urine from 2 to 3 major calyces (which in turn drain 7 to 13 minor calyces). It tapers inferiorly at the ureteropelvic junction (UPJ).
renal_pelvis.function: Acts as a primary collection funnel channeling filtered urine from the calyces into the ureter for expulsion into the urinary bladder.
renal_pelvis.clinical: Ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) obstruction causes hydronephrosis (swelling of the renal pelvis and calyces) that can permanently damage renal parenchyma if untreated.
facts: Funnel-shaped conduit within the renal sinus
Formed by the convergence of major calyces
Smooth muscle in pelvis walls exhibits peristaltic contractions
Susceptible to renal calculus (kidney stone) impaction

renal_artery.name: Renal Artery
renal_artery.description: Large paired blood vessels that branch laterally off the abdominal aorta below the superior mesenteric artery. The right renal artery is longer and passes posterior to the IVC.
renal_artery.function: Delivers approximately 1 to 1.2 litres of blood per minute (~20-25% of resting cardiac output) directly into the kidneys for filtration, nutrient supply, and gas exchange.
renal_artery.clinical: Renal artery stenosis (caused by atherosclerosis or fibromuscular dysplasia) diminishes perfusion, triggering excessive renin release and renovascular hypertension.
facts: Right renal artery is longer than the left and passes behind the IVC
Carries ~20-25% of cardiac output directly to kidneys
Divides into anterior and posterior segmental branches at the hilum
Features no significant anastomoses between segmental branches

renal_vein.name: Renal Vein
renal_vein.description: Short, wide veins that drain purified venous blood from the kidneys directly into the inferior vena cava. The left renal vein is longer and crosses the aorta beneath the superior mesenteric artery.
renal_vein.function: Carries filtered, deoxygenated blood devoid of metabolic wastes back into the systemic venous circulation for return to the right atrium.
renal_vein.clinical: Nutcracker syndrome occurs when the left renal vein is compressed between the abdominal aorta and SMA, causing left flank pain, pelvic congestion, and hematuria.
facts: Left renal vein is 3× longer than right and crosses anterior to the aorta
Left gonadal and left suprarenal veins drain into the left renal vein
Drains into the inferior vena cava (IVC)
Compression causes Nutcracker syndrome

ureter.name: Ureter
ureter.description: A muscular duct (~25-30 cm in length) running retroperitoneally down the posterior abdominal wall from the renal pelvis into the posterior wall of the urinary bladder.
ureter.function: Transports concentrated urine from the renal pelvis to the urinary bladder via rhythmic, myogenic peristaltic contractions of its smooth muscle muscularis layer.
ureter.clinical: Nephrolithiasis (kidney stones) migrating down the ureter often lodge at three anatomical narrowings (UPJ, pelvic brim, and UVJ), causing excruciating ureteric colic pain.
facts: Propels urine via smooth muscle peristalsis, not gravity alone
Has three physiological narrowings prone to stone impaction
Enters bladder obliquely to create a one-way physiological anti-reflux valve
Lined by specialized transitional epithelium (urothelium)

adrenal_gland.name: Adrenal Gland (Suprarenal)
adrenal_gland.description: Triangular endocrine gland capping the superior pole of each kidney, enveloped within renal fascia. Comprises an outer steroid-producing cortex and an inner catecholamine-secreting medulla.
adrenal_gland.function: Secretes mineralocorticoids (aldosterone), glucocorticoids (cortisol), androgens, and sympathetic catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine) into systemic circulation.
adrenal_gland.clinical: Addison's disease causes adrenal cortex insufficiency, while Cushing's syndrome results from hypercortisolemia. Pheochromocytoma is a tumor of the adrenal medulla causing hypertensive crises.
facts: Right gland is pyramidal; left gland is semilunar and slightly larger
Cortex derived from mesoderm; medulla derived from neural crest
Medulla acts essentially as a modified sympathetic ganglion
Essential for salt retention, glucose regulation, and fight-or-flight response

quiz.question: Approximately what percentage of resting cardiac output is delivered to the kidneys via the renal arteries?
quiz.explanation: The kidneys receive approximately 20-25% of the total resting cardiac output (~1.2 L/min), reflecting their tremendous filtration workload.

quiz.question: Which anatomical layer of the kidney contains all the renal corpuscles (glomeruli and Bowman's capsules)?
quiz.explanation: All glomeruli and initial ultrafiltration filtration barriers reside within the outer renal cortex and renal columns.

quiz.question: What hormone produced by the adrenal cortex regulates sodium retention and potassium excretion in the distal tubules?
quiz.explanation: Aldosterone, a mineralocorticoid secreted by the adrenal zona glomerulosa, acts on distal nephron collecting tubules to promote sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion.

quiz.question: By what mechanism is urine propelled through the ureters from the kidneys to the bladder?
quiz.explanation: The smooth muscular coat of the ureters generates rhythmic waves of peristalsis (2-6 per minute) that actively propel urine droplets into the bladder, functioning even when lying flat or upside down.

quiz.question: Compression of the left renal vein between the abdominal aorta and superior mesenteric artery is known clinically as:
quiz.explanation: Nutcracker syndrome is the anterior entrapment of the left renal vein between the abdominal aorta and SMA, often presenting with left flank pain, pelvic congestion, and hematuria.
